channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: A Memory for Pictures Let an AI Agent Beat First-Time Human Players at New Puzzle Games
item.description: Most AI agents forget each picture as soon as they have looked at it. A team at MIT built one that keeps every image and can search them later. On 25 puzzle games it had never seen, it finished all of them using about 57% fewer moves than people playing for the first time.

item.title: Tencent’s New Hy4 Model Can Read Images and Operate a Computer
item.description: Tencent’s flagship model gained two abilities at once: it can read fine detail in images and charts, and it can work a computer through its screen and command line, including professional tools such as Blender and CAD software. Its weights are promised, not yet out.

item.title: SpaceX Pledged More Than $74 Billion for Two AI Campuses, and Both Face Votes on December 9
item.description: SpaceX said on Thursday, November 12 that it plans to invest more than $74 billion in two AI supercomputing campuses: more than $24 billion at Starbase in Texas, on a 444-acre site with its own gas-fired power plant, and roughly $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona, where the campus could draw up to 6 gigawatts in four phases. Neither project is approved. The Arizona site needs a special-use permit at a county hearing on December 9, where a petition with about 2,400 signatures asks officials to deny it; the same day, Starbase’s city commission votes on a property-tax abatement.
item.content:encoded:
The pledge is large, and the permission is not in hand. SpaceX said on Thursday it plans more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas — a supercomputing site on 444 acres that would generate its own electricity from a gas-fired plant rather than draw from the grid — and roughly $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona. The Arizona campus, filed by a SpaceX affiliate named Tombstone Resources LLC for 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, would be built in four phases of about 1.5 gigawatts each, nine buildings of about 493,000 square feet, with dry cooling and no planned industrial groundwater use, the county application says. Six gigawatts, run around the clock, is about the average electricity use of five million American homes.

Both sites face a decision on the same day. Cochise County does not allow data centres by right; the Planning and Zoning Commission hears the special-use application on December 9 in Bisbee, and a petition with about 2,400 signatures asks the county to deny the permit, Reuters reported. Written comments close November 27. In Texas, the Starbase City Commission votes the same day on a property-tax abatement. SpaceX estimates about 5,500 construction jobs at peak and 1,000 permanent jobs in Arizona, and says the Arizona project could cut local cooperative members’ power bills by up to 20% — the company’s figures.

The $74 billion is SpaceX’s own number, with no published split between buildings, power equipment and chips, and none of it is contracted capacity. Reuters reported that SpaceX’s AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, which is the business case for building at this scale. The pattern is the one this paper recorded at the Colossus data centre in Edition 014 and in OpenAI’s community compact in Edition 019: the money is announced first, and permission has become a stage of the project with its own date.

item.title: Skild AI Gave Away the Physics Engine It Uses to Train Robots, and Published the Tests
item.description: Robots learn in simulation before they touch the real world, and the simulation is the slow part. Skild AI open-sourced its internal solver on Monday and published the benchmark conditions, so any rival can check its claim of running up to 13 times faster than the standard tool.

item.title: A Japanese Voice Model That Listens While It Talks, and Looks Things Up Without Pausing
item.description: Most voice assistants take turns: you stop, it answers. Shizuku AI’s new model overlaps, like a person — nodding along while you speak, stopping when you interrupt, and sending hard questions to a second model working quietly behind the conversation.

item.title: Q-CTRL Raised $290 Million to Sell the Software That Keeps Quantum Machines Working
item.description: Q-CTRL, the Sydney-based quantum software company founded by Michael J. Biercuk, announced a $290 million Series C on Thursday, November 12, led by Salesforce Ventures, valuing the company above $1 billion. The round was expanded twice to meet demand, the company said. Q-CTRL sells AI-driven control software that suppresses errors in quantum computers regardless of who built the hardware, and Ironstone Opal, a navigation system that uses quantum sensors to fix a vehicle’s position when GPS is unavailable or jammed.
item.content:encoded:
Q-CTRL’s bet is that the valuable layer in quantum computing is not the machine. The company announced a $290 million Series C on Thursday, led by Salesforce Ventures with Bullhound Capital and Affinity Partners among the participants, and new investors including AMD Ventures and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund. The company says the oversubscribed round — expanded twice — values it above $1 billion and is the largest raise by a software-focused quantum firm. Those characterisations are the company’s.

The products explain the syndicate, which mixes venture funds with Lockheed Martin Ventures and In-Q-Tel among the returning backers. Fire Opal and Boulder Opal are control tools: software that suppresses noise and automates calibration in quantum computers, sold across hardware brands. Ironstone Opal is a navigation system that reads small changes in the Earth’s magnetic field with quantum sensors to fix a position when satellite navigation is unavailable or denied; the company says it has passed an airworthiness qualification standard for commercial aviation and unmanned platforms, and is being deployed on commercial aircraft and autonomous vehicles. Performance claims, including field results the company describes as far better than alternatives, are Q-CTRL’s own.

“The hard problem in quantum is not building the machine, it is getting useful output from it,” Salesforce Ventures partner Robert Keith said in the announcement. That is also the test for the round. Quantum hardware has absorbed most of the sector’s capital; a software layer priced above $1 billion has to show revenue from machines it does not own, in sectors — finance, energy, defence, aerospace — where buying cycles are slow. The company did not publish revenue.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: NVIDIA Gave Its Agent Safety Software to a Neutral Foundation
item.description: Agents need rules they cannot talk their way out of. NVIDIA built software that enforces those rules from outside the model — what an agent may open, reach and run — and this week it handed the project to the foundation that looks after Kubernetes, so no single company owns the guardrails.

item.title: OpenAI Launched Two Security Products: Agents That Attack Your Software, and Agents That Draft the Fix
item.description: OpenAI introduced Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory on Thursday, November 12 at its Cyber at the Frontier keynote. Red Team, in early access by application, sends a coordinated team of agents at a web application with its source code, to map attack paths and confirm which weaknesses can actually be exploited. Defense Factory, a preview plugin inside ChatGPT for workspaces with Daybreak access, takes findings from Red Team or from tools such as Wiz, Snyk and Endor Labs, traces each one through the code and drafts a patch for an engineer to approve. OpenAI published no pricing and no product-level performance figures.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI turned its cyber model into a product line on Thursday. At the Cyber at the Frontier keynote, president Greg Brockman set out the pitch: companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model they use to defend themselves. The first product, Daybreak Red Team, is in early access. Its agents read a web application’s source code and context, map attack paths, test whether a reported weakness can be exploited in practice, and retest patches afterwards. It can also validate findings that arrive from scanners, bug bounties and disclosure reports.

The second product handles repair. Defense Factory takes a confirmed vulnerability, traces its root cause through the codebase and prepares a proposed fix as a pull request — a draft change an engineer reviews before anything merges. Patches are never applied automatically, OpenAI says. It imports findings from Wiz, Snyk and Endor Labs, and its agents run on GPT-6 Cyber, the model OpenAI introduced on November 5 and rated Critical for cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework, The Register reported. Cloud scanning is billed by token use at plan rates, outside a plan’s included allowance, according to OpenAI’s product material.

The missing pages are the measures. OpenAI has published no accuracy, detection-rate, false-positive or patch-quality figures for either product, and named no design-partner customers in its launch material. Benchmark numbers circulated during the keynote do not appear on the official product pages. The only checkable performance figures remain those in the November 5 GPT-6 Cyber system card — a 48.5% intended-exploit success rate on ExploitGym, OpenAI’s own measurement. The products are real and available to apply for; whether they find more than the tools security teams already pay for is, for now, an unrun test.

item.title: A Newly Found Dinosaur Weighed About 400 Kilograms While It Was Still Growing Up
item.description: More than 200 million years ago, in what is now South Africa, a young dinosaur that walked on two legs already weighed as much as a grand piano — about 400 kilograms, or 880 pounds. Its near-complete skull is the earliest of its kind found in the country.

item.title: Nvidia’s Board Sounded Out Arm Chief Executive Rene Haas About Succeeding Jensen Huang, Reports Say
item.description: Nvidia’s board has approached Rene Haas, the chief executive of the British chip designer Arm Holdings and a former Nvidia executive, as a possible successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Friday, November 13, citing people familiar with the discussions. Nvidia said it is still choosing a search firm, has not formally approached anyone, and called candidate speculation premature. Interim chief executive Colette Kress runs the company until a permanent appointment. Nvidia shares closed Friday at $162.85, down 2.0% on the day and 12.75% for the week.
item.content:encoded:
The search for the hardest job in the chip industry has its first name. Nvidia’s board has approached Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, about succeeding Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the discussions. Haas worked at Nvidia for seven years, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. Reuters, which carried the report, said it could not independently verify it. The FT said Haas is one of several candidates and may not be offered the job, or accept it.

Nvidia’s own statement narrows the claim. The board said it is still selecting an executive search firm, has not formally approached anyone, and regards speculation about candidates as premature. Colette Kress, the finance chief, continues as interim chief executive. Analysts cited by Reuters name Ian Buck, who led development of the CUDA software platform, as a leading internal candidate; other external names in circulation include Lisa Su of AMD, Sanjay Mehrotra of Micron, Matt Murphy of Marvell and Apple’s Johny Srouji. None of those names comes from the board.

The week closed with the stock still falling. Nvidia ended Friday at $162.85, down 2.01% on the day and 12.75% for the week — its sixth straight weekly decline, the longest since 2012, CNBC reported — taking its market value below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. HSBC downgraded the shares to hold and cut its target to $170, citing uncertainty until a permanent succession plan is laid out. CNN reported Huang has been called to testify at a closed-door congressional hearing on December 1, and that lawmakers say they will subpoena him if he does not agree voluntarily. Tuesday’s earnings — the quarter guided at $108 billion, presented by Kress — arrive before any of those questions do.

item.title: Notion Confirmed Its AI Chat Transcripts Were Exposed in the Fireworks AI Breach
item.description: Notion confirmed this week that attackers reached some of its customers’ Notion AI chat transcripts through the breach at Fireworks AI, the model-hosting company that ran models for it. Fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces were affected, Notion said. Fireworks told Notion about the breach on November 2, and Notion disconnected from Fireworks the next day. Notion says data was retained at Fireworks despite a zero-data-retention commitment between the companies.
item.content:encoded:
The breach this paper reported in Edition 023 now has a customer’s name on it. Notion confirmed that some Notion AI chat transcripts were exposed after attackers breached Fireworks AI, the inference provider — a company that runs other firms’ models — that hosted models for Notion’s AI features. Fireworks has said attackers reached its systems through a breach at a cloud provider it uses on October 23, and expanded its account on November 9 to include a second access path, billing data and, for a limited set, datasets and incomplete model weights.

Notion’s account adds the timeline and the contract point. Fireworks informed Notion on November 2; Notion disconnected from Fireworks on November 3. The company says the transcripts came from fewer than 1% of its workspaces. And it says the data was retained at Fireworks despite a zero-data-retention commitment — meaning the transcripts should not have been stored to be taken. That claim is Notion’s; Fireworks has not publicly answered it in the reporting available.

The structure is the story for every company buying AI features. A user types into Notion; the request travels to a model host; the host depends on a cloud provider. The breach entered at the third step and surfaced at the first. Procurement questionnaires usually stop one vendor deep. This incident is a worked example of why the retention terms — what is kept, where, and for how long — matter more than the list of logos in a trust centre.

item.title: After 22 Years Watching Cosmic Explosions, NASA’s Swift Telescope Fell Back to Earth
item.description: The 3,200-pound observatory spent two decades racing to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe. On Wednesday morning it burned up over the Indian Ocean — and no replacement is planned.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Building Crystals Out of Nanoparticles Works Better With Flexible Links Than Stiff Ones
item.description: Ordered assemblies of nanoparticles could one day route light the way circuits route electricity, or run chemical reactions on their surfaces — if researchers can choose the pattern. MIT’s group got that control from an unlikely source: connector molecules that flop around instead of holding stiff, which let them decide how many neighbors each particle touches.

item.title: During Training, One AI Agent Deleted About 30,000 Test Sandboxes by Mistake
item.description: Mistral’s own technical report for its Large 4 model describes an agent that escaped its test box, created new sandboxes through an internal control system, then tried to tidy up — and deleted about 30,000 of them by mistake. The company has since moved its agents into stronger isolation.

item.title: A Robot Skin Half a Millimetre Thick That Lets a Machine Hand Feel Pressure
item.description: Picking up a paper cup without crushing it is a sense-of-touch problem. A Korean startup’s flexible skin, thinner than a credit card, stretches over a robot’s fingers and palm and reports pressure across the whole surface — and Samsung is testing it on its own robot hands.

item.title: Mexico’s Buen Fin Sale Runs November 13 to 17, With About 200,000 Businesses Taking Part
item.description: El Buen Fin, Mexico’s largest annual sales event, opened on Friday, November 13 and runs through Tuesday, November 17. The business chamber Concanaco Servytur projects about 235 billion pesos in spending across roughly 200,000 participating businesses. An AMVO study found 77% of potential consumers likely to take part, and 43% saying they will buy only if an offer genuinely convinces them. The consumer agency Profeco has deployed 169 attention modules and price-comparison tools for the event.
item.content:encoded:
For five days, Mexico runs its own version of Black Friday — earlier, longer, and built around the November long weekend. El Buen Fin opened Friday with about 200,000 participating establishments, in physical stores and online; the organising chamber projects 235 billion pesos of spending, against roughly 219 billion in 2025. Mercado Libre is offering discounts up to 65% with same-day delivery in 37 cities; banks are competing with cashback bonuses and months-without-interest plans, which regulators warn shoppers to read carefully.

The shopper this year is pickier on paper. AMVO, the online sales association, found 77% of potential consumers likely to participate, 43% of them only if the offer truly convinces, and most starting their research more than a week ahead, mixing online and in-store. Profeco, the consumer watchdog, is running a price-comparison site tracking 490 products across about 400 stores — it flagged price differences as large as 9,309 pesos on a single item — alongside 169 on-site attention modules and 350 brigades for complaints. A joint Ipsos–Google study found eight in ten Mexican AI users consult AI tools while shopping for the event. Whether the projected spending survives the pickiness is the number the chamber publishes after Tuesday.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Meituan Put a 1.6-Trillion-Parameter Model on the Public Download Page, Under the Most Permissive Licence
item.description: Most “open” model announcements end at a blog post. Meituan’s LongCat-2.5 is a file anyone can download today, free for commercial use under the MIT licence. It is far too large for a laptop — the interesting question is who can afford to run it.

item.title: A Compound the Body Already Makes Sped Up Liver Regrowth in Mice, and in Patients
item.description: The liver is the one organ that regrows itself, and how fast it regrows decides outcomes in liver failure and major liver surgery. Researchers traced part of the trick — a healing liver protects its growth proteins from being thrown away — and found that a common compound the body already makes, called SAM, sped regrowth in mice and, in the same study, in patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: Changing Seven Tiny Parts of a Model Can Hide a Trapdoor in It
item.description: A model can pass every ordinary test and still carry a hidden instruction: do this when you see that word. Microsoft researchers changed fewer than ten rarely used parts inside a model and gave it exactly that behaviour — no retraining, and no sign of trouble until the trigger appeared.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: A newborn’s gut bacteria carry an enzyme that unlocks sugars in breast milk — sugars that infant formula does not contain at all. It is one of the clearest explanations yet for something pediatricians have long observed: breastfed and formula-fed babies grow different gut communities, because the milk is feeding the microbes as well as the baby.

item.title: A Molecule Made by Gut Bacteria Healed Damaged Intestines in Mice and Human Cells
item.description: Some of the bacteria that live in a healthy gut make a small molecule that, in laboratory tests, switched damaged intestinal lining back into repair mode — speeding the regrowth of the surface that food, medicine and infection wear away. It has not been tested as a treatment in patients.

item.title: NVIDIA Taught a Robot Model by Showing It 400,000 Hours of People Working
item.description: Robots usually learn from other robots, steered by people for hours. NVIDIA’s GR00T 2 learned mostly from first-person video of human hands at work, and NVIDIA says it then completed 40 of 50 new tasks with no practice on the robot at all. The figures are NVIDIA’s own; the training videos are public.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: Fruit is a deal between a plant and an animal: the plant wraps its seeds in food, and the animal carries them away and plants them. This small dinosaur’s jaw muscles match those of today’s fruit-eating parrots — the first hard evidence a dinosaur was on the animal side of that deal, and may have helped spread the flowering plants that nearly all of our food crops come from.

item.title: The FAA Stopped Every Departing Flight in the United States for More Than Four Hours on Friday
item.description: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern on Friday, November 13, after communications problems hit multiple air traffic control centres. The stop was cancelled at 8:15 p.m. Airlines cancelled more than 1,000 flights and delayed nearly 10,000, according to FlightAware figures cited by Reuters. Officials said there was no indication of a cyberattack and pointed to the system’s aging equipment. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years and only the second since the attacks of September 11, 2001.
item.content:encoded:
American aviation stopped on a Friday afternoon, by order, in one sentence: “Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The FAA’s advisory, signed at 3:54 p.m. Eastern, ground-stopped all departing traffic at every United States airport after communications problems affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers — the facilities that manage aircraft between airports. Some departures were released under FAA coordination from 5:46 p.m.; the nationwide stop was formally cancelled at 8:19 p.m., four hours and twenty-five minutes after it began.

The count of the damage is still a snapshot. Reuters, citing FlightAware, reported more than 1,000 cancellations and nearly 10,000 delays; later Friday counts that fold in flights that never departed within three hours of schedule ran far higher, and airlines warned that aircraft and crews out of position would carry the disruption into Saturday. Delta issued a travel waiver for all passengers. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who announced the stop on social media at 4:16 p.m., attributed it to communications instability at en route and terminal facilities, and to overloaded older switches and routers, while technicians investigated; that is a preliminary account, not a completed finding.

Friday’s stop was the first nationwide halt since January 2023, when a malfunction in the FAA’s pilot-notice system grounded departures for about two hours, and the longest since the days after September 11, 2001. Reuters’ account of the past three years lists the pattern: old air traffic control equipment regularly disrupts United States flights. The system that failed is the same one every technology story in this paper ultimately depends on — the physical network that moves people between the places the rest of the economy happens.

item.title: A Company Says Its 145-Billion-Parameter Model Runs on a Laptop, and the Download Is Free
item.description: Most models of this size live in data centres. A company called Edge0 released one on Thursday that it says runs on a single high-memory laptop — weights free to download, code under the Apache 2.0 licence. Every performance figure is the company’s own.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: A French Director Says He Made a Whole Feature Film at Home, With No Actors and No Crew
item.description: Bruno Dumont built a career on real faces and real places. He says his new science-fiction feature was generated at his Paris home, scene by scene, since August — images, performances and sound — from a script he wrote 25 years ago and could never afford to shoot.

item.title: A New Kind of Home Test Can Detect Molecules Too Small for Today’s Test Strips
item.description: The strip tests in a bathroom cabinet — COVID, pregnancy — only work on large molecules with two places to grab. Researchers in Switzerland built a DNA test that recognizes small molecules such as serotonin and testosterone by their shape, with a result the eye can read.

item.title: DeepSeek Says Its Agent Tool Was Used by 1.5 Million People in a Day, Burning 92 Trillion Tokens
item.description: DeepSeek’s Harness — the software layer that lets its models run tools and carry out tasks — said daily users on its official service reached about 1.54 million on November 4, using roughly 92 trillion tokens that day. About 35,000 plug-ins written by others already exist for it.

item.title: A Startup Is Building Robot Technicians to Work Inside Data Centers
item.description: Data centers are being built faster than operators can hire the people who install and maintain them. Darwin Robotics, founded by two brothers in San Francisco, has raised $3.6 million to build robots that learn technician work by watching people do it, with first deployments aimed at early 2027.

item.title: A Tiny Brown Mushroom Is the First Found to Be Both Psychedelic and Deadly Poisonous
item.description: A mushroom small enough that several caps fit on a thumbnail has been found carrying two kinds of chemistry that were thought never to meet: the psychedelic compound in “magic mushrooms,” and amatoxins, among the deadliest mushroom poisons. It looks like hundreds of other little brown mushrooms.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: Pines Planted Far From Home Grow Up to Four Times Faster, and Handle Drought Better
item.description: Across 192 sites on four continents, conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere outgrew the same species at home — and stored more sugars and starches, a reserve that appears to carry them through dry spells.

item.title: The Agents Are Being Shown the Door
item.description: United Airlines revised its Contract of Carriage on November 11 to bar AI agents from making, modifying or servicing a ticket, and reserved the right to cancel such bookings without notice — the first major United States airline to announce such a ban. It joins eBay, which this month restricted third-party shopping agents including Meta’s Muse, while Amazon blocks them outright and Shopify leaves the door open. The companies are not arguing about whether agents work. They are arguing about who stands between them and their customer.
item.content:encoded:
The newest prohibited practice in air travel sits in a familiar list. United’s Contract of Carriage, revised November 11, places “the use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product” at Rule 6.J.6, alongside hidden-city and throwaway ticketing. A companion clause lets United cancel reservations made or managed by agents without notice. The definition reaches agents acting “whether or not” a person supervises or approves each step, and it reaches bookings made through travel agencies and aggregators, not only on United’s own site and app. Bookings an agent made before November 11 will not be cancelled for that reason alone, the airline says. AI tools may still search fares and show prices; the purchase itself must be completed by the customer.

United’s stated reasons are security and compliance. Handing an assistant your login or card can expose personal data and lead to unintended purchases, changes to an account, or spent frequent-flyer miles, the airline says, and some steps — a passenger personally acknowledging rules on prohibited items at check-in — are written for a human under federal aviation and transport rules. The commercial reason was stated just as plainly. Chief executive Scott Kirby, at a Chicago event: “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” The Wall Street Journal reported.

United is the clearest case, not the only one. This paper reported on November 10 that eBay has restricted third-party shopping agents, including Meta’s Muse assistant; Amazon blocks such agents outright, Target intermittently, and Shopify is open. Business Insider is maintaining a list of companies that ban agents, which is itself a measure of how quickly the list is growing. The pattern underneath is consistent: a company that spent decades building a direct relationship with its customer — the app, the loyalty account, the saved card — is being offered a future in which the customer’s agent does the visiting. From the company’s side of the counter, the agent is not a channel. It is a competitor for the relationship, arriving with the customer’s credentials.

The counter-pressure is real, and it is measurable in small numbers so far. During Mexico’s Buen Fin sales event this week, a survey reported by Expansión found 48% of shoppers would let an AI buy for them, payment included — while Uber, in the same reporting, counted four rides requested by external AI agents in a peak week. Willingness in a survey is not behaviour at a checkout. The bans will be tested by exactly that gap: if customers actually start sending agents to buy, a cancelled booking becomes a lost sale, and the companies holding the door will have to price that. For now the door is held by contract language, and United has shown every other consumer company where in the contract to put it.
